idiom_name: newtype forwarding (explicit impl or Deref) + OnceLock/LazyLock for virtual proxies
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so a proxy is a newtype that holds the subject and either implements the same trait by forwarding to self.inner (explicit, checked by the compiler) or implements Deref/DerefMut so the wrapper transparently behaves like the subject (smart reference; Box/Rc/Arc cover ownership and sharing, RefCell/Mutex/RwLock add checked interior mutability for locking and caching proxies). The virtual-proxy kind is standard library territory: OnceLock::get_or_init and LazyLock defer and memoize initialization, including across threads. Implement Deref only when the wrapper is genuinely pointer-like - the std documentation warns that deref coercion is a footgun for inheritance-style APIs and that leaked methods can surprise users.
pitfalls: Deref-based proxies expose the whole inner API (methods and coercion targets), which the std docs call out as undesirable for non-pointer-like types; prefer an explicit trait impl when the proxied surface should stay small.
LazyLock/LazyCell initialization that panics poisons the cell permanently - every later access panics, unlike Mutex poisoning which can be recovered with into_inner.
Interior mutability changes the type's Send/Sync story: Rc/RefCell are single-threaded, and holding a Mutex guard across .await in async code deadlocks - use tokio::sync primitives there.
Deref proxies can make method resolution ambiguous: an inherent method on the wrapper and one on the target can shadow each other in ways that are hard to read.
